title: Show the requester's overlay address and the paired device it would replace
body:
## Summary
The approval card a person decides from shows only what the requester asserted (name, kind, grants); the pending record keeps no channel-stamped address, and approving a request whose asserted device_id is already paired silently replaces that device's row and kills its token.

## Description
Registry device-pairing/pairing-ceremony: 'who is asking - the claimed display name *and* the channel-stamped identity, both rendered fully' and 'the asserted identity must come from the channel, not the payload'. src/athena/peer/routes.py:80-114 (pair_request) never reads request.client; src/athena/peer/pairing.py:142-150 (pending_view) carries pairing_id, name, kind, requested_grants, expires_at, pair_back only; pairing.py:271 sets peer_id = record.device_id (requester-supplied) and listener.py admit -> registry.py:192-221 `self._rows[peer_id] = row` replaces any earlier row for that id. Fixed looks like: PairingRecord keeps the socket address of the request (routes.pair_request passes request.client), pending_view exposes `address` and `replaces: {peer_id, name} | null`, and the desktop approval card (apps/desktop/src/scenes/mind/devices.tsx, out of this round's paths) renders both, with a visible warning on `replaces`.

## Flow
- an overlay member that read a pairing code types it and sends device_id = an already-paired PC's id and name = that PC's name
- the Devices page shows 'Desk asks to be let in' - identical to a legitimate re-pair
- the person approves; registry.admit replaces Desk's row, Desk's real token now gets 401 and Desk's link reads removed_there
- fix order: record address in pairing.request, add address/replaces to pending_view + TS PendingView mirror, render in devices.tsx, tests both sides

## Expected impact
The person approving a PC sees which overlay address asked and whether approving evicts a device they already trust. Could break: the desktop PendingView mirror and its fixtures must gain two fields in the same change.

## Evaluation
Claim: quality - the mint gate shows the channel-stamped identity and the eviction it causes
Before: 0 of 2 facts on the approval card (address, replaces); pending_view keys counted at pairing.py:143-150
After: 2 of 2, pinned by a pytest on pending_view and a devices.test.tsx render case
Method: simulation - walked the code path above; the fix spans the desktop renderer and its TS mirror, outside this round's write set
Result: unmeasurable
Gate: contract
evidence:
src/athena/peer/pairing.py:142-150 pending_view keys: pairing_id, name, kind, requested_grants, expires_at, pair_back
src/athena/peer/routes.py:89-98 request() called without request.client
src/athena/peer/pairing.py:271 record.peer_id = record.device_id or ids.mint('device')
src/athena/peer/registry.py:218-220 self._rows[peer_id] = row (replaces)
instrument: pytest: pending_view carries `address` (the PeerRequest.client of the request) and `replaces` (the existing row's name when device_id matches a live row); desktop devices.test.tsx renders both on the approval card

title: Answer pre-trust refusals after a fixed delay, as timing-defenses asks
body:
## Summary
Every refusal on the peer listener's pre-trust surface (wrong_code, wrong_nonce, wrong_secret, unauthorized) is answered at natural speed; the device-pairing standard's timing-defenses technique asks for a fixed artificial delay on the failure path.

## Description
Registry device-pairing/timing-defenses, 'The fixed-delay refusal': failed authentication answers after a fixed delay, wrong and unknown alike, so online guessing is throttled without lockout state. src/athena/peer/listener.py:295-306 returns 401 at once; src/athena/peer/routes.py:74-77 (_refused) returns the pairing refusals at once. The code's own guess budget (pairing.py WRONG_LIMIT, a 30-bit code) bounds the code path, so the gain is defence in depth; the cost is a handler thread held for the delay per refusal on a ThreadingHTTPServer, which is why this is not built unread.

## Flow
- an overlay member sends GET /peer/hello with random bearer tokens: each 401 returns in ~1 ms
- a code guesser sends POST /peer/pair/request: each wrong_code returns at once (closing windows after 5)
- fix: one REFUSAL_DELAY_S constant on the failure path of _dispatch's 401 and of _refused, documented beside REFUSAL

## Expected impact
Online guessing against tokens and codes slows by the delay factor; a legitimate typo waits a fraction of a second. Could break: thread exhaustion if many refusals arrive at once - the instrument must measure it.

## Evaluation
Claim: resilience - refusal latency is uniform and floored
Before: 401 and wrong_code answered in ~1 ms (no delay constant exists; listener.py:295-306, routes.py:74-77)
After: every refusal >= the constant, successes unchanged, thread count bounded under 32 concurrent refusals
Method: simulation - the delay trades guess rate against held handler threads; only a socket-level instrument can show both
Result: unmeasurable
Gate: policy-tighten
evidence:
src/athena/peer/listener.py:297-306 peer_error(401, 'unauthorized', ...) returned immediately
src/athena/peer/routes.py:74-77 _refused -> peer_error immediately
grep -n 'sleep\|DELAY' src/athena/peer/listener.py src/athena/peer/routes.py -> no match
instrument: pytest over a real peer socket: a wrong_code / wrong_nonce / wrong_secret / 401 answer takes >= the documented delay, a success does not, and 32 concurrent refusals hold no more than the listener's thread budget

title: Write an audit row for every mint, claim, revoke and pre-trust refusal
body:
## Summary
Granting, claiming and withdrawing trust leave no durable record: the only trace is one stderr line for claim_spent; approvals, revocations, lapses and refusal causes vanish when the process ends.

## Description
Registry device-pairing/timing-defenses, 'the ledger gets everything': the refusal the caller sees is uniform, the record the defender writes carries the true cause, the peer address, the presented identity and the time. src/athena/peer/devices.py:302-338 (answer_pending, revoke) and listener.py:540-554 (tick lapse) change who may enter and write nothing but peers.json; routes.py:126-130 logs claim_spent to stderr only; listener.py:295-306 refusals record nothing. So 'a surface under attack and a surface nobody visits' are indistinguishable to the defender afterwards. Fixed: an append-only $ATHENA_HOME/peer/audit.jsonl (write_whole is for snapshots; this wants an append with fsync) with one row per act, no secrets, bounded by rotation.

## Flow
- a person approves a phone, later revokes it; a day later nothing on disk says when either happened
- an overlay member burns five wrong codes: the window closes and no row says why
- fix order: an audit writer module, rows at approve/decline/claim/revoke/lapse/refusal, a test per act, atlas omission line for the new module

## Expected impact
The person (or a later investigation) can answer who was let in when, who was removed, and whether anyone probed the pairing doors. Could break: a write on the refusal path adds I/O to the pre-trust surface; rotation must bound it.

## Evaluation
Claim: quality - every trust change and refusal leaves a record
Before: 0 of 7 acts (approve, decline, claim, claim_spent, revoke, lapse, refusal) write an audit row; 1 of 7 (claim_spent) writes a stderr line
After: 7 of 7 write one row each, none containing a secret (pinned by tests)
Method: simulation - a new module and file format; M with a new artefact, not landed unread
Result: unmeasurable
Gate: policy-tighten
evidence:
grep -rn 'audit' src/athena/peer -> no match
src/athena/peer/routes.py:127-129 the only record: _log(f'claim_spent: ...')
src/athena/peer/devices.py:335-338 revoke -> host.revoke, no record
src/athena/peer/listener.py:542-544 lapse revokes the row, no record
instrument: pytest: approve, decline, claim, claim_spent, revoke, lapse and each pre-trust refusal append exactly one row (cause, pairing or peer id, remote address, time) to the peer audit file, and no row contains a token, nonce or claim secret

title: Keep the peer tick's reap and reconcile off its outbound pair-back calls
body:
## Summary
PeerHost.tick() runs the outbound pair-back delivery and every pending join's claim poll inline, each a blocking call with a 5 s timeout, before it reaps rows and reconciles the listener, so one unreachable PC stretches every 2 s tick to 5 s or more per stuck call.

## Description
src/athena/peer/listener.py:540-554: sweep, reap, then `for record in self.pairings.undelivered(): self.deliver(record)` (client.call, CALL_TIMEOUT_S = 5.0) and `_poll_joins()` (one call per pending join, same timeout), then reconcile. An approved pair-back is retried every tick until it lapses (WINDOW_TTL_S after approval); a join polls until 2 x WINDOW_TTL_S. With the other PC asleep behind a dropped SYN, each tick blocks ~5 s per record, so the beacon going off, a window expiring or an overlay address change reaches the listener late by that much. Authentication itself is not delayed (expiry is checked at authenticate), which keeps this a liveness risk, not a security hole. Fixed: run delivery and join polling on their own worker (or with a short per-tick budget) so sweep/reap/reconcile keep their cadence.

## Flow
- PC A approves a pair-back for PC B, then B sleeps (overlay drops packets)
- every A tick spends ~5 s in deliver() before reconcile; turning the beacon off takes ~5-7 s to close the listener instead of <= 2 s
- two such records or a stuck join double it

## Expected impact
Listener lifecycle and expiry reaping keep their 2 s cadence whatever the network does. Could break: delivery/claim ordering against sweep - the worker must not deliver a lapsed token.

## Evaluation
Claim: resilience - tick cadence independent of peer reachability
Before: tick wall time ~= 2 s + 5 s per unreachable pair-back or join (simulation from CALL_TIMEOUT_S and the loop at listener.py:540-554)
After: tick wall time <= tick_s with a stuck peer, measured by the instrument
Method: simulation - needs a blackholed socket and a timed tick; concurrency change, M risk 4
Result: unmeasurable
Gate: none
evidence:
src/athena/peer/listener.py:547-551 deliver() and _poll_joins() inline in tick()
src/athena/peer/client.py:312 CALL_TIMEOUT_S = 5.0
src/athena/peer/listener.py:533-538 one tick thread
instrument: pytest: a pair-back whose deliver_to is a socket that accepts and never answers; measure tick() wall time and the delay before an expired row is reaped and the listener reconciled (Before ~5 s per stuck call, After <= tick_s)

title: Scope the phone page's live region to the conversation, not all of main
body:
## Summary
<main id="app" aria-live="polite"> makes every change inside the page a polite announcement: each streamed text.delta that settle() rewrites into her message, every step line, every redrawn panel.

## Description
src/athena/peer/mobile/index.html:24 puts aria-live on <main>; app.js settle() (app.js:420-424) rewrites the current message's textContent on every delta, so a screen reader is handed a growing paragraph again and again while a turn streams; renderChat() and show() replace whole subtrees inside the same region. The banner (role=alert) and the status line (role=status) are already their own regions. Fixed: drop aria-live from <main>; make the conversation `role="log"` (implicit polite, additions only) and announce a settled message once, at turn.finished, rather than each delta.

## Flow
- VoiceOver/TalkBack user sends a message
- her answer streams in ~20 deltas; each settle() rewrites the text node inside the live region
- the reader queues partial sentences instead of the answer once

## Expected impact
A screen-reader user hears each answer once and each card once. Could break: the pairing panels lose their implicit announcement unless their headings take focus.

## Evaluation
Claim: user - announcements per turn
Before: every delta of a streamed answer re-announced (one per text.delta, walked from app.js settle)
After: one announcement per finished message, counted by the harness
Method: simulation - no DOM harness for app.js exists; it is the instrument to build
Result: unmeasurable
Gate: none
evidence:
src/athena/peer/mobile/index.html:24 <main id="app" aria-live="polite">
src/athena/peer/mobile/app.js:420-424 settle() rewrites node.textContent per delta
src/athena/peer/mobile/app.js:370 banner role=alert already separate
instrument: a jsdom harness for app.js (jsdom is in node_modules) that counts text inserted under aria-live regions during one scripted streamed turn and one cards poll; axe over the chat view

title: Forget the phone's token in memory too when the beacon removes it
body:
## Summary
After the beacon answers 401, revoked() -> forget() clears storage and timers but leaves chat.saved holding the dead token, and the visibilitychange listener ready() added keeps calling /peer/hello and /peer/decisions with it.

## Description
src/athena/peer/mobile/app.js:271-277 forget() clears localStorage, sessionStorage and the intervals, not chat.saved; app.js:345-350 the visibilitychange handler runs `if (document.visibilityState === "visible" && chat.saved) { hello(); loadCards(); }` and is never removed. Each wake of a removed phone sends two requests with a revoked bearer, each 401 re-runs revoked() and redraws the 'removed' panel. Fixed: forget() sets chat.saved = null (and the handler is added once).

## Flow
- the person removes the phone in Devices
- the phone's next poll gets 401 and shows 'This phone was removed'
- each time the phone screen wakes: GET /peer/hello and GET /peer/decisions with the old token, two 401s on the beacon, the panel redrawn

## Expected impact
A removed phone goes quiet instead of knocking with a dead token on every wake. Could break: nothing visible; the panel stays.

## Evaluation
Claim: quality - requests sent with a revoked token after revocation
Before: 2 per wake (walked from app.js:345-350)
After: 0, counted by the harness
Method: simulation - app.js runs start() at import and touches document, so it needs the jsdom harness card above
Result: unmeasurable
Gate: none
evidence:
src/athena/peer/mobile/app.js:271-277 function forget() { ... } (no chat.saved = null)
src/athena/peer/mobile/app.js:345-350 visibilitychange -> hello(); loadCards() when chat.saved
instrument: the same jsdom harness for app.js: a 401 on /peer/hello, then a visibilitychange to visible - count the requests that still carry the old bearer (Before >= 2 per wake, After 0)

title: Let old wrong codes age out instead of closing a later pairing window
body:
## Summary
PairingBook counts wrong codes for the daemon's whole life (`_wrong_codes`), so typos from yesterday close today's open window on its first mistyped code.

## Description
src/athena/peer/pairing.py:396-403: every unmatched code increments one counter that resets only when it reaches WRONG_LIMIT (5), then closes every OPEN window. Nothing ages it: four typos across a week plus one today expire a window the person just opened. A sliding count (wrong codes in the last WINDOW_TTL_S) keeps the per-window bound - a window lives WINDOW_TTL_S, so it still faces at most WRONG_LIMIT wrong codes - while forgetting guesses older than any live window. It is routed to a person because it lets the daemon accept wrong codes over a longer span than today (a policy-loosen in letter, even though the per-window guess bound is unchanged).

## Flow
- on Monday the person mistypes a code four times across two joins
- on Friday they open a window; the other PC's first typo is the fifth wrong code - the window closes at once
- the second PC's correct retry gets wrong_code; the person must open another window

## Expected impact
Joins with honest typos stop failing on stale counts. Could break: an attacker spacing guesses gets WRONG_LIMIT per window rather than per lifetime-cycle - the same bound the docstring already claims.

## Evaluation
Claim: user - a fresh window survives stale typos
Before: 4 stale wrong codes + 1 new close a fresh window (probe: PairingBook with a Clock, 4 wrong, advance a week, open, 1 wrong -> window_open() False)
After: the same sequence leaves the window open; 5 wrong within one window still close it
Method: probe - Before taken on a PairingBook with an injected clock (4 wrong codes, +4 days, open, 1 wrong -> wrong_code and window_open() False); After is the sliding count as designed, not built here because it is policy-loosen
Result: better
Gate: policy-loosen
evidence:
src/athena/peer/pairing.py:160 self._wrong_codes = 0 (process lifetime)
src/athena/peer/pairing.py:396-402 self._wrong_codes += 1; at WRONG_LIMIT every OPEN window -> EXPIRED; no time component
